source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 solved the Gick and Holyoak radiation problem by analogy. Alone it gave the direct-ray solution; after the general story it gave the convergence solution.
numbers: Single-problem demonstration (supplement S5.1-S5.2); no solve rate reported.
limits: Story and target were in the same context window. In the authors' words, once the context is emptied it reverts to the non-analogical solution.
agent_relevance: Zero-shot analogy from a source held in context works. Nothing persists unless our memory re-supplies the source.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: With two distractor stories added, GPT-3 lost the convergence solution, as humans do. Told to consider the earlier stories, it picked the general story and solved it.
numbers: Supplement S5.4-S5.5. Qualitative, one problem.
limits: Mirrors the human hint effect (Gick and Holyoak 1980). Authors note GPT-3 has no episodic long-term memory.
agent_relevance: O7 should not rely on spontaneous retrieval among many items. An explicit 'consider the stored lessons' step restores transfer (bridging).

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Text digit-matrix reasoning (Raven-like): GPT-3 beat the human average (N=40 UCLA undergraduates) on all problem types. Its pattern of difficulty matched humans.
numbers: Generative: odds ratio 1.88, p=0.005, CI [1.21,2.91]. Multiple choice: OR 6.27, p=2.3e-8. Profile correlation r(30)=0.39, p=0.027. Best human got every problem right.
limits: Within-task relational mapping, so near transfer. Not a test of transfer across domains.
agent_relevance: Relational mapping inside a prompt is strong; the weak part is finding and carrying sources across contexts.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Letter-string analogies with permuted or symbol alphabets. Humans stayed high. GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 fell sharply on counterfactual alphabets.
numbers: Accuracy over all alphabets, listed order in the table: humans 0.753 [0.734,0.773]; then 0.488, 0.350, 0.452 for the three GPT models (GPT-3, 3.5, 4 as labelled in the table). 1,876 human samples; 6,840 per model. Human accuracy did not fall with more permuted letters; model accuracy fell, with a second sharp drop for symbols.
limits: Letter-string domain only. Model labels in the extracted table were ambiguous, so the model order is as printed.
agent_relevance: A model that transfers by structure should not lose accuracy when surface symbols change. Test lesson reuse with surface-swapped copies.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Partial failed replication of Webb et al.: on Webb's original problems the GPT models scored generally below the human average in this setup.
numbers: Humans higher on most problem types except Add Letter (and Remove Redundant for GPT-3).
limits: Authors say protocol and participant pool may explain the difference; their humans scored higher than Webb's.
agent_relevance: Do not treat 'LLMs beat humans at analogy' as settled. Check per benchmark.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Reasoning or Reciting? Counterfactual tasks
finding: 11 task pairs (default vs counterfactual, e.g. base-10 vs base-9 arithmetic). Across GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude and PaLM-2, counterfactual scores were above chance but consistently and substantially below default.
numbers: GPT-4 gpt-4-0314 plus three other models. Zero-shot CoT helped some tasks and not others. Default and counterfactual scores were correlated.
limits: Same procedure with changed surface mapping is a clean far-transfer probe. Some skill is general, part is tied to the default condition.
agent_relevance: A stored lesson may help partly because it matches familiar surface forms. Check lessons on counterfactual variants.

source: Sourati, Ilievski, Sommerauer, Jiang (2024) ARN: Analogical Reasoning on Narratives (TACL)
finding: Near vs far analogy between narratives. Models are good at near analogies and poor at far ones. GPT-4 was below random on far analogies.
numbers: Overall human 96.0 vs model average 57.3 (random 50). Near analogies: humans 97.9, models 75.0. Far analogies: humans 94.1, models 39.6. Plain SBERT similarity reached 77.9 in the near setting.
limits: Binary choice of analogy vs distractor; GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama-2, FlanT5, Macaw. 1.1k triples.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM far-analogy recognition is weak. Far analogues need a typed mapping check, as SCHEMA O7 already says.

source: Sourati et al. (2024) ARN
finding: Near distractors (high surface overlap, wrong structure) wreck model performance. In the hardest cell, a far analogy against a near distractor, the model average was 33.9%.
numbers: Partition averages 76.9 / 73.2 / 45.3 / 33.9 (humans 98.6 / 97.2 / 96.8 / 91.4). Humans dropped little; models dropped a lot.
limits: Column labels for the four cells were in the paper's table; I read them as near-vs-near down to far-vs-near.
agent_relevance: Surface-lure effect is the Gick and Holyoak surface-over-structure retrieval bias, stronger in models. Embedding retrieval of lessons will favour surface twins.

source: Sourati et al. (2024) ARN
finding: Solved examples and chain-of-thought improved model analogy accuracy but did not close the gap to humans on far analogies.
numbers: Demonstrations chosen randomly; three runs averaged; Llama-2, GPT-3.5, GPT-4.
limits: Exact per-condition gains not recorded this session.
agent_relevance: Prompt scaffolds help partly, least on far transfer.

source: Stevenson, Pafford, van der Maas, Mitchell (2025) Can LLMs generalize analogy solving like children can?
finding: Letter-string analogies in Latin (base), Greek (near transfer) and symbol (far transfer) alphabets. Children and adults did not lose accuracy across alphabets. All four LLMs did.
numbers: Alphabet effect: adults F(1.59,96.9)=0.95, children F(2,76)=0.27, both n.s. Claude-3.5 F=29.5, Gemma-2 27B F=88.2, GPT-4o F=55.0, Llama-3.1 405B F=135.0, all p<.001. Zero-shot, same prompts as for children.
limits: A rule-check control showed some failures are rule-knowledge gaps (second successor) but not all (predecessor item).
agent_relevance: Clearest recent human-vs-LLM near/far transfer result. Children generalise; LLMs do not. The scaffold must carry the abstraction.

source: Stevenson et al. (2025) Can LLMs generalize analogy solving like children can?
finding: Item-level accuracy in the pooled item table shows rule novelty drives failure: on item 5 (predecessor rule) GPT-4o scored 0.39, Claude-3.5 0.20, children 0.38, adults 0.81.
numbers: Table 4. Item 1: adults 0.97, children 0.85, GPT-4o 0.92. Item 3: adults 0.82, children 0.52, GPT-4o 0.45.
limits: Table 4 pools alphabets; read it as rule difficulty, not alphabet effect.
agent_relevance: Transfer fails first on less common rules, not only on unfamiliar symbols.

source: Hodel and West (2023) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models (known only via Lewis and Mitchell, Stevenson et al.)
finding: Reported that GPT-3 performance degraded on letter-string analogies with shuffled alphabets, a challenge to Webb et al.
numbers: Not opened. Described in two papers I did read. The arXiv id is from memory and unchecked.
limits: Second-hand.
agent_relevance: Counterfactual probes keep showing a drop, so treat Webb-style success as in-distribution.

source: Gick and Holyoak 1983 Experiment 2, as restated in the 2025 strategic-decisions paper
finding: Human baseline restated: 29% (8 of 28) solved the radiation problem unaided and 50% (14 of 28) after a hint to use the story.
numbers: Quoted from the 2025 paper, not from the 1983 paper.
limits: Second-hand figures for a primary study.
agent_relevance: Assume no spontaneous transfer in humans or models. Add an explicit retrieval and 'use it' step.

source: Can LLMs help improve analogical reasoning for strategic decisions? Humans vs GPT-4 (2025)
finding: Two-source, two-target matching version of Gick and Holyoak with business problems. Humans (n=199) vs GPT-4 (60 runs). GPT-4 solved more problems, but its analogy use was less accurate.
numbers: Humans: factory problem solved 6.3% unhinted and 8.7% (4 of 46) hinted; HR problem 20.3% unhinted and 37% (17 of 46) hinted. Lower than the 1983 baseline, which the authors attribute to the extra matching step.
limits: Business context, one-shot, small cells. Human solve rates are low.
agent_relevance: Matching among several candidate sources is where human transfer breaks down.

source: Can LLMs help improve analogical reasoning for strategic decisions? Humans vs GPT-4 (2025)
finding: GPT-4 with no hint almost never used the Radiation analogy for the factory problem (1 of 15 runs, 6.7%). With a hint all 15 did. For the Dolphin source it used it unhinted in 14 of 15.
numbers: n=15 per cell. The hint made an analogy's existence explicit without naming it.
limits: Whether an analogy was 'used' is self-reported by the model.
agent_relevance: A one-line 'an analogy may apply' hint flips model use from near zero to all. Cheap scaffold for impasses.

source: Can LLMs help improve analogical reasoning for strategic decisions? Humans vs GPT-4 (2025)
finding: Precision/recall split. GPT-4 has recall near 1.0 but precision about 0.5 (false positives on the distractor). Humans have precision up to 1.0 but recall as low as 0.06 (Radiation) and 0.22 (Dolphin).
numbers: Unhinted humans: Radiation precision 0.42, recall 0.06, F1 0.11; Dolphin precision 1.00, recall 0.22, F1 0.36. GPT-4 errors came from surface similarity; human errors from wrong abstraction.
limits: Self-reported source choice may inflate model recall.
agent_relevance: Design: let the LLM propose many candidate analogues (high recall), then use a code or second-pass structural check to filter (precision).

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners (ICLR)
finding: Analogical prompting: ask the model to recall relevant problems and solutions itself, then solve. It beat 0-shot CoT and few-shot CoT on math and code. Reported average gain: 4 points.
numbers: GSM8K: GPT-3.5-turbo 5-shot CoT 75.0 vs self-generated 75.8; text-davinci-003 14.8 vs 50.3; PaLM2 60.8 vs 78.2. MATH: GPT-3.5 33.0 vs 33.9; PaLM2 27.1 vs 29.8.
limits: Gain tiny on GPT-3.5, large on weaker models. Exemplars need no labels.
agent_relevance: Cheap in-loop self-generated analogue step. Mild effect on strong models, so do not oversell.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners (ICLR)
finding: BIG-Bench with GPT-3.5: gains uneven across tasks.
numbers: Temporal sequences: 3-shot CoT 44.8 vs self-generated 58.0. Logical deduction 35.2 vs 36.4. Colored objects 61.6 vs 62.0. Word sorting 67.6 vs 68.4. Formal fallacies 55.6 vs 55.6.
limits: Ties on several tasks.
agent_relevance: Treat analogical prompting as a helper where examples are missing, not a general booster.

source: Wang, Mao, Fried, Neubig (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Agent induces reusable workflows from past tasks and abstracts example-specific values into slots (e.g. {product-name}). This is explicit abstraction for transfer.
numbers: WebArena: +51.1% relative success over BrowserGym baseline (12.0 absolute points). Mind2Web cross-task: +24.6% relative step success.
limits: GPT-4 web agents. Task-level success on Mind2Web stays 0.7 to 4.8 percent.
agent_relevance: Closest AI analogue of bridging: strip surface details from past successes before reuse.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Transfer gradient. Online induction (from test queries) generalises better as the domain gap grows; offline induction is close to it in-domain.
numbers: Mind2Web step SR, GPT-4: MindAct cross-task 36.2, cross-website 30.1, cross-domain 18.6; AWM offline 45.1 / 33.7 / 32.6; AWM online 43.6 / 33.9 / 35.5.
limits: Task SR is tiny, so step SR is the usable number.
agent_relevance: Near-transfer gain is large; far-transfer gain is real but smaller. Matches the human near/far gradient.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners (AAAI)
finding: Insights extracted on HotpotQA were reused on FEVER, a different task. They helped.
numbers: FEVER success: ReAct 58%; ExpeL Transfer without task demos 63 (+/-0.4); ExpeL Transfer 65 (+/-1.7). One further table value, 70 (+/-0.7), could not be labelled from my text extraction.
limits: One source-target pair, both fact-checking QA families.
agent_relevance: Cross-class lesson reuse works modestly (+5 to +7 points) when the lesson is abstract insight text.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL
finding: Diversity of experience matters: failure/success pairs gathered with Reflexion beat ReAct-only experience, and insights mattered most on HotpotQA.
numbers: Figure 6 and Fig 5 comparisons; exact numbers not recorded because my table extraction was misaligned.
limits: Qualitative reading.
agent_relevance: Contrast pairs (fail vs succeed) are the best source of abstractable lessons. This parallels variability of practice in humans.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: an open-ended embodied agent with LLMs
finding: A skill library of code skills reused in a new world on unseen tasks. Voyager solved all four tasks in 3 of 3 trials; ReAct, Reflexion and AutoGPT solved none within 50 iterations.
numbers: Iterations, with library: Diamond Pickaxe 19, Golden Sword 18, Lava Bucket 21, Compass 18. Without library 36 (2/3), 30, 27, 26. AutoGPT using Voyager's library: 1/3, 1/3, 0/3, 2/3.
limits: Minecraft only; skills are executable code composed from earlier skills; 3 trials each.
agent_relevance: Executable, composable skills with descriptions transfer well and are plug-in for other agents.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Buffer of Thoughts
finding: A meta-buffer of high-level thought templates is retrieved and instantiated per task. Large gains on structurally repetitive puzzles.
numbers: GPT-4: Game of 24 3.0 standard, 74.0 ToT, 82.4 BoT; Checkmate-in-One 36.4 vs 86.4; Geometric Shapes 52.6 vs 93.6; Date Understanding 68.4 vs 88.2. Reported cost about 12% of multi-query methods.
limits: Tasks are template-friendly and buffer is built on the same task families, so gains may be near transfer.
agent_relevance: Abstract template, retrieve, instantiate: the schema-reuse pattern. Gains come from near-class reuse.

source: Ouyang et al. (2026) ReasoningBank (ICLR)
finding: Stores strategies distilled from successes and failures. Beat memory-free agents and raw-trajectory memory, including in cross-site and cross-domain settings.
numbers: WebArena success +8.3, +7.2, +4.6 over memory-free across three backbones. SWE-Bench-Verified Gemini-2.5-flash 34.2 to 38.8; pro 54.0 to 57.4. WebArena Multi subset (transfer across sites): +4.6 over best baseline while AWM did not help.
limits: Mind2Web task success is tiny (cross-domain 1.0 to 1.6, Gemini flash).
agent_relevance: Abstracted strategy memory beats stored trajectories as transfer distance grows. Gains are modest.

source: Huan et al. (2025) Does math reasoning improve general LLM capabilities?
finding: Over 20 open reasoning-tuned models: most that gained on math failed to carry gains to other reasoning or non-reasoning tasks. In a controlled Qwen3-14B study RL on math transferred; SFT on math often did not.
numbers: Transferability Index metric. SFT models often had a negative non-reasoning index. Figure 1: SFT changes on non-reasoning tasks reached about -29.5 points; RL on other reasoning reached +15 to +20.
limits: Open-weight models, math-only data; SFT schedules were short per Ren et al.
agent_relevance: Modern far-transfer finding: training on one domain rarely transfers far. Argues for scaffold-level reuse over fine-tuning.

source: Ren et al. (2026) Rethinking generalization in reasoning SFT (COLM)
finding: Counter to Huan et al.: SFT cross-domain generalisation is conditional. Short training shows a dip then recovery. Verified long-CoT traces give consistent cross-domain gains. Strong models gain; weak ones copy verbosity.
numbers: Qwen3-14B-Base, Math-CoT: MATH500 77.8 to 95.1, GPQA-D 44.1 to 63.3, LCB v2 37.5 to 55.1, MMLU-Pro 61.8 to 74.4. Lower-quality NuminaMath hurt: LCB 37.5 to 20.4. Qwen3-8B Math-CoT LCB only 29.1 to 31.0. Safety falls after long-CoT SFT.
limits: Base models only.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: far transfer depends on learning the procedure (backtracking, verification), not content, and on model strength.

source: Ren et al. (2026) Rethinking generalization in reasoning SFT (COLM)
finding: Procedural transfer: long-CoT traces from the toy Countdown game improved math, code and science benchmarks on strong models.
numbers: Qwen3-14B Countdown-CoT: AIME24 14.7 to 41.7, GPQA-D 44.1 to 53.0, MMLU-Pro 61.8 to 65.4, LCB 37.5 to 43.8. Qwen3-8B: AIME24 12.0 to 26.0, LCB 29.1 to 32.8.
limits: Smaller effect in the 8B model.
agent_relevance: Supports abstraction by procedure (backtrack, verify) as the transferable part.

source: Forbus, Gentner, Law (1995) MAC/FAC: a model of similarity-based retrieval (seen only in search results)
finding: Two-stage retrieval: cheap surface-based first pass, then structural match on the few survivors. Explains why human retrieval is surface-biased while judged soundness is structural.
numbers: No numbers recorded this session.
limits: My search found no LLM benchmark built on MAC/FAC.
agent_relevance: Natural recipe for O7: embedding recall, then a typed structural check.
